summary.text: A phase transition is a change of a substance from one state to another, most often among solid, liquid and gas.
It happens when conditions such as temperature or pressure change, and some properties can jump abruptly, like the volume when a liquid turns to gas.
At the exact transition point the two phases are equally likely to exist, and on either side one of them is the more stable.

facts.label: What triggers it
facts.value: A change in temperature or pressure

facts.label: Boiling jump
facts.value: Liquid turning to gas changes volume abruptly

facts.label: Phase diagram
facts.value: Shows the most stable phase at each temperature and pressure

facts.label: Solid to solid
facts.value: A crystal can change structure without changing chemistry

facts.label: Magnetic example
facts.value: Ferromagnet to paramagnet at the Curie point

items.prompt: A pot of water sits at the exact temperature where steam and water are equally ready to exist. What is true of the two forms there?

options.label: They have identical free energies, so neither is favored
The water is more stable until the pot empties
The steam is always the more stable of the two
Only one can exist until the heat is turned up

items.explain: At the transition point the two phases have identical free energies, so they are equally likely to exist.

items.prompt: A pot of water is held just under its boiling point. Which form of the water is the more stable one?

options.label: The vapor, because it holds more energy
Neither, since both are equally stable there
The liquid, because the temperature is below boiling
The vapor, because pressure favors it

items.explain: Below the boiling point the liquid is the more stable state; above it the gas is.

items.prompt: Very clean water is chilled a few degrees past its freezing point and stays unfrozen. How is this state best described?

options.label: Unstable, so it must freeze immediately
Metastable: less stable than ice, yet not unstable
Fully stable, the same as ice at that point
A plasma, because it passed the transition

items.explain: Supercooling carries a system past a transition point without the transition; the result is metastable.

items.prompt: Carbon, a pure element, rearranges from one crystal structure to another with no change in chemistry. What is this kind of change called?

options.label: Polymorphism
Supersaturation
A eutectic transformation
Allotropy

items.explain: In elements a change of crystal structure is allotropy; in compounds it is polymorphism.

items.prompt: A magnetic material switches from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic. What is the temperature of this change called?

options.label: The Curie point
The boiling point
The spinodal point
The eutectoid point

items.explain: The ferromagnetic to paramagnetic transition occurs at the Curie point.

items.prompt: A lab heats a pure compound and watches it melt. What is typical of a chemically pure compound?

options.label: It melts across a span where solid and liquid coexist
It has separate liquidus and solidus temperatures
It melts at a single temperature
It melts only when pressure is also changed

items.explain: Pure compounds show one melting temperature, while mixtures may have a span between solidus and liquidus.

paragraphs.heading: What a phase transition is
paragraphs.text: A phase transition, or phase change, is a medium shifting from one state to another. Most often the phrase means a move between solid, liquid and gas, and now and then plasma. Within a single phase, the physical properties are uniform throughout. When outside conditions such as temperature or pressure change, some of those properties change too.

paragraphs.heading: Sudden jumps
paragraphs.text: The change can be abrupt. Heat a liquid to its boiling point and it becomes a gas, with a sudden jump in volume. The conditions at which such a change happens are called the phase transition point. At the boiling point, liquid and gas have identical free energies, so each is equally likely; below it the liquid is the more stable of the two, and above it the gas is.

paragraphs.heading: Phase diagrams
paragraphs.text: For a single substance, a phase diagram maps which phase is most stable at each temperature and pressure, usually showing states in equilibrium. A transition normally happens when changing conditions carry the system across from one region to another, as when water freezes once it drops below the freezing point. Sometimes, though, a system can be pushed past a transition point without changing phase. It is then metastable: less stable than the phase it would have become, but not unstable either. Superheating and supercooling are examples, and such states do not appear on ordinary phase diagrams.

paragraphs.heading: Solid to solid
paragraphs.text: A solid can also take on a different structure without changing its chemical makeup. In elements this is called allotropy, and in compounds polymorphism. Moving from one crystal structure to another, from a crystal to an amorphous solid, or between amorphous structures all count. In carbon steel, the martensitic transformation is one of many such changes and serves as a model for displacive transformations.

paragraphs.heading: Magnetic order
paragraphs.text: The idea reaches beyond states of matter to kinds of magnetic ordering. The best known case is the switch between the ferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases of magnetic materials, at what is called the Curie point. A simplified but very useful model of such magnetic transitions is the Ising model.

paragraphs.heading: Mixtures
paragraphs.text: Mixtures and solutions behave in more complicated ways than a single compound. A chemically pure compound melts at one temperature, but a mixture may either melt at one point, called congruent melting, or melt across a span of temperatures in which solid and liquid exist together in equilibrium. Some transitions involve three phases. In a eutectic transformation, a liquid made of two components cools and turns into two solid phases.

paragraphs.heading: Further examples
paragraphs.text: Certain metals and ceramics become superconducting when cooled below a critical temperature. Liquid crystal phases are an in-between stage, or mesophase, between solid and liquid. And in spinodal decomposition, a single phase that is cooled separates into two different compositions.
